story: Shinkei Systems puts its PSDN-S computer-vision harvesting robot on Cook Inlet salmon boats during the 2026 sockeye season while the branded Seremoni product is processed and sold outside Alaska

claims.claim: IntraFish published an article headlined 'Shinkei rolls out robot-harvested Alaska salmon' on 22 July 2026.
claims.verbatim: Shinkei rolls out robot-harvested Alaska salmon
claims.notes: Body is paywalled. Only headline, subhead, byline (Rachel Sapin), timestamps, photo caption and tags are readable. Cite only as what IntraFish published on its public page, never as reported body text.

claims.claim: IntraFish's subhead says Shinkei expects to roll out its Seremoni Grade salmon to select retail and restaurant partners this summer.
claims.verbatim: Shinkei expects to roll out its 'Seremoni Grade' salmon to select retail and restaurant partners this summer.
claims.notes: An expectation, not a shipped product. As of 2026-07-29 seremoni.com listed no salmon or sockeye, so the deck must not say the retail product is on shelves.

claims.claim: IntraFish's photo caption places Shinkei Systems working with fishermen in Alaska's Cook Inlet in 2026.
claims.verbatim: Shinkei Systems working with fishermen in Alaska's Cook Inlet in 2026. Photo: Matt Lowber
claims.notes: This caption plus the company LinkedIn post are the only Cook Inlet evidence confirmed on a fetched page. Shinkei's own homepage contains no mention of Alaska, Cook Inlet or sockeye.

claims.claim: Shinkei Systems announced PSDN-S as its newest harvesting robot created to bring Seremoni Grade handling to Alaska's wild salmon industry.
claims.verbatim: Meet PSDN-S, Shinkei's newest harvesting robot, created to bring Seremoni Grade handling to Alaska's wild salmon industry.
claims.notes: Primary company statement. The post carries a relative timestamp read on 2026-07-29, so the date is derived rather than printed.

claims.claim: Shinkei says PSDN-S was built to make its harvesting technology more practical for the smaller boats used throughout Alaska's salmon fisheries.
claims.verbatim: PSDN-S was created to make our harvesting technology more practical for the smaller boats used throughout Alaska's salmon fisheries.
claims.notes: Primary. The same post continues that expanding access to Seremoni Grade handling can bring wild sockeye salmon to more tables.

claims.claim: Shinkei chief executive Saif Khawaja said the company owns the machines and puts them on the boats for free.
claims.verbatim: We own the machines and put them on the boats for free.
claims.notes: Bylined Paul Molyneaux, dated August 6 2025 on the page. The article contains no Alaska mention.

claims.claim: Khawaja said Shinkei splits the proceeds variably with the fishermen it works with.
claims.verbatim: We split it variably with the fishermen we work with.
claims.notes: This cuts against a simple extraction thesis and must be carried, not buried. The terms of the split are not disclosed anywhere fetchable.

claims.claim: Khawaja said Shinkei handles and markets the fish under its own brand Seremoni Grade.
claims.verbatim: We handle and market the fish under our brand, Seremoni Grade.
claims.notes: The strongest verified support for the branding half of the thesis.

claims.claim: Shinkei's lead mechanical engineer Waiman Meinhold described the deck machine as about the size of a refrigerator.
claims.verbatim: It's about the size of a refrigerator,
claims.notes: Describes the earlier PSDN unit, not necessarily the Alaska PSDN-S.

claims.claim: Shinkei says the machine scans a fish, spikes the brain, cuts the gills and puts it into slush ice in 6.5 seconds or less.
claims.verbatim: It'll scan a fish, spike the brain, cut the gills, and then put it into slush ice, all in 6.5 seconds or less.
claims.notes: Consistent with The Spoon's about six seconds. Do not present 6 and 6.5 as competing numbers.

claims.claim: Khawaja said Shinkei can build a machine every two weeks.
claims.verbatim: We can build a machine every two weeks,
claims.notes: A build rate as of mid-2025. Do not project a current fleet size from it.

claims.claim: The Spoon reported that each fish is processed in about six seconds.
claims.verbatim: each fish is processed in about six seconds
claims.notes: Bylined Michael Wolf.

claims.claim: The Spoon reported that Shinkei uses computer vision AI to scan the fish and determine the fastest and least stressful path forward.
claims.verbatim: uses computer vision AI to scan the fish to determine the fastest (and least-stressful) path forward
claims.notes: This is the AI claim the deck rests on. Vendor-described capability reported by a trade outlet, never independently tested. Prefer the company says framing.

claims.claim: The Spoon reported that a traditionally suffocated fish enters rigor mortis in about 7 hours while Shinkei's process expands that up to 60 hours.
claims.verbatim: in about 7 hours, but Shinkei's process expands that up to 60 hours
claims.notes: Company-supplied figures. Attribute to Shinkei via The Spoon.

claims.claim: The Spoon reported that Shinkei recently raised 22 million dollars in a Series A co-led by Founders Fund and Interlagos.
claims.verbatim: recently raised $22 million
claims.notes: Corroborated independently by National Fisherman and by RobotToday. The larger 30 million dollar cumulative figure could not be verified verbatim and was killed.

claims.claim: The Spoon reported that Shinkei works with eight boats sourcing black cod, rockfish and red snapper.
claims.verbatim: works with eight boats, sourcing species like black cod, rockfish
claims.notes: December 2025, predating the Alaska rollout. The deck must NOT claim a number of Cook Inlet boats. No fetched source states how many Alaska vessels carry PSDN-S.

claims.claim: Shinkei acquired a 16,000 square foot fish processing facility in Tacoma, Washington from FATHOM Seafood.
claims.verbatim: 16,000-square-foot fish processing facility
claims.notes: Independently corroborated by Robotics and Automation News, same square footage, seller and city. Load-bearing for the processed outside Alaska half of the thesis.

claims.claim: The Tacoma plant was reported to open in spring 2026 with a core workforce of more than 50 employees plus seasonal hires.
claims.verbatim: core workforce of more than 50 employees, with additional seasonal hires
claims.notes: Written as a forward-looking plan in March 2026. No source confirms the plant is now operating at that headcount. Use was expected to.

claims.claim: Shinkei said the Tacoma plant would source fish from fishermen in Alaska, Washington and California.
claims.verbatim: Alaska, Washington, and California
claims.notes: Corroborated by SalmonBusiness. Attribute rather than quote at length.

claims.claim: Khawaja said NERA uses Shinkei's proprietary datasets to show how fresh each fish is and how many days it can be sold.
claims.verbatim: With NERA, we use our proprietary datasets to provide unprecedented visibility into each fish's journey: how fresh it is, when it reaches peak quality and how many days it can be sold.
claims.notes: The second AI system in the story, and the one that sits at the Tacoma plant rather than on the Alaska boat.

claims.claim: Shinkei's website says PSDN extends shelf life 3x.
claims.verbatim: PSDN extends shelf life 3x
claims.notes: Undated marketing page. A vendor claim with no published methodology. The homepage also carries the stress response that degrades 70% of fish quality, 6 different species and counting, Five U.S. Regions and an El Segundo California address, and contains NO mention of Alaska, Cook Inlet or sockeye.

claims.claim: Khawaja told the Los Angeles Times his end goal is grocery shoppers buying fish that lasts three times as long, tastes better and is handled humanely.
claims.verbatim: My end goal is that you're walking into your local grocery store and can buy fish that lasts three times as long, tastes better and is handled humanely.
claims.source_outlet: Los Angeles Times republished by AOL
claims.notes: Bylined Piper Heath, exactly one year before this run. The stated goal is a grocery store, not a dock price.

claims.claim: The Alaska Department of Fish and Game says more than 1,300 drift and set gillnet limited entry permits exist for the Upper Cook Inlet area.
claims.verbatim: More than 1,300 drift and set gillnet limited entry fishing permits
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Department of Fish and Game
claims.notes: Undated agency page. The same sentence adds that these are about 10% of salmon permits issued statewide. Use for honest scale.

claims.claim: The Alaska Department of Fish and Game says sockeye salmon are the most important species by economic value in Upper Cook Inlet.
claims.verbatim: Sockeye salmon are most important in terms of their economic value.
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Department of Fish and Game

claims.claim: NOAA Fisheries says the 2026 commercial fishing season for the Cook Inlet EEZ Area opens on June 22 and closes on or before August 15.
claims.verbatim: The 2026 commercial fishing season for the Cook Inlet EEZ Area will open on June 22 and will close on or before August 15.
claims.notes: These dates govern the FEDERAL Cook Inlet EEZ Area only. They are NOT the state-waters Upper Cook Inlet drift and set gillnet season.

claims.claim: The Alaska Department of Fish and Game reported the 2025 statewide commercial salmon harvest at 194.8 million fish worth approximately 541 million dollars.
claims.verbatim: The 2025 commercial salmon fishery harvest for all species was valued at approximately $541 million, a significant increase from $304 million in the 2024 season.
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Department of Fish and Game
claims.notes: The same release gives sockeye at 53 million fish and 315 million dollars of value. It does NOT print per-species per-pound prices.

claims.claim: Deckboss reported that the 2025 Upper Cook Inlet sockeye harvest was worth 35.8 million dollars at an estimated average price of 1.73 dollars per pound.
claims.verbatim: At an estimated average price of $1.73 per pound, the total ex-vessel value for the sockeye harvest was $35.8 million.
claims.notes: The ONLY Cook Inlet specific ex-vessel price verified on a fetched page. Explicitly an estimate, 2025 not 2026, from a one-person fisheries blog. Must be hedged and dated. The same post gives the commercial harvest as 3.7 million sockeye.

claims.claim: KFSK reported that Silver Bay Seafoods announced a Bristol Bay sockeye base price of 1.60 dollars per pound for the 2026 season.
claims.notes: DO NOT let this stand in for Cook Inlet. The article never mentions Cook Inlet. It also reports Southeast dock sockeye at about 3.00 dollars per pound, showing how wide the regional spread runs.

claims.claim: Trade coverage of the Alaska rollout says Shinkei provides its robots to Alaskan fishermen at no cost while purchasing their catch at premium prices.
claims.verbatim: at no cost while purchasing their catch at premium prices
claims.notes: Weakest sourcing in the set and the claim that most complicates the thesis. Corroborated by FISHBIO's republication of the IntraFish piece. The no-cost half is independently supported by Khawaja's own quote. Use reportedly, and say the premium is undisclosed.

claims.claim: FISHBIO reported Khawaja saying the company is doing the equivalent of surgery on the fish in a very difficult maritime environment.
claims.verbatim: We're basically doing the equivalent of surgery on these fish in a very difficult maritime environment.
claims.notes: Returned identically across two separate fetches. FISHBIO is retelling a paywalled IntraFish story. Attribute as Khawaja told IntraFish, as reported by FISHBIO.

killed.claim: Shinkei has raised 30 million dollars in total funding as of July 2025
killed.why: No verbatim string captured on the AOL republication of the Los Angeles Times piece. The verified funding number is the 22 million dollar Series A.

killed.claim: Shinkei operates four Poseidon robots with plans for ten more within a year
killed.why: No verbatim string captured, and stale as of July 2025.

killed.claim: The Los Angeles Times reported planned expansion into Alaskan and Gulf of Mexico waters
killed.why: Returned only as paraphrase, no verbatim. Tempting for the deck's arc and unprovable.

killed.claim: Shinkei processes thousands of pounds weekly across Washington, Central California and Massachusetts
killed.why: No verbatim on the AOL page. National Fisherman's a few thousand pounds a week is a different, older and smaller figure and is not a substitute.

killed.claim: Any retail price for Seremoni-brand fish
killed.why: seremoni.com publishes no prices. No fetchable page gave a per-pound or per-portion retail figure. The deck must NOT state a commodity-to-retail spread.

killed.claim: 2026 Upper Cook Inlet sockeye ex-vessel price paid to fishermen
killed.why: Does not exist on any reachable page. Cook Inlet processors had not published a 2026 base price in anything fetchable.

killed.claim: 2025 statewide Alaska average prices of Chinook 6.40, sockeye 1.17, coho 1.41, pink 0.30, chum 0.80 dollars per pound
killed.why: The ADF and G 2025 harvest summary explicitly does not print per-species per-pound prices, and the exvessel price reports render dynamically. Unverified, so all five die.

killed.claim: The Upper Cook Inlet drift gillnet season runs June 25 to the end of August, peaking mid to late July
killed.why: Could not be confirmed on any fetched page. The only verified season dates cover the federal Cook Inlet EEZ Area, a different management area.

killed.claim: Counts of Upper Cook Inlet drift gillnet permits that made deliveries in 2025
killed.why: Available only as a search-engine snippet of a PDF, which house rules forbid citing.

killed.claim: Fast Company's feature on the Cook Inlet salmon robot
killed.why: fastcompany.com returned HTTP 403. The article's existence is confirmed indirectly by Shinkei's own LinkedIn post thanking Fast Company and Clint Rainey, but no content from it may be used.

killed.claim: Undercurrent News, Shinkei adds sockeye to high-end Seremoni seafood offerings
Shinkei's own website says it operates in Alaska or Cook Inlet or handles sockeye
killed.why: It does not. shinkei.systems was fetched twice and seremoni.com once on 2026-07-29. Neither mentions Alaska, Cook Inlet or sockeye, and Seremoni's species list is Black Sea Bass, Black Cod, Red Snapper, Vermilion Rockfish, Porgy and Blackgill Rockfish with no salmon.

killed.claim: National Fisherman's Robots on Deck was published 2026-01-01
killed.why: The page states August 6 2025, byline Paul Molyneaux. Every claim drawn from it is background from mid-2025.

notes: ADVERSARIAL READ. The event is real and in window, and it is thinner than the brief assumed. Verified in-window material amounts to an IntraFish headline, subhead and photo caption behind a paywall, one company LinkedIn post, and two secondary retellings of that same paywalled article. There is no primary document, no agency filing, no fisherman interviewed on a readable page, and no number for how many Cook Inlet boats carry PSDN-S. The deck must say a handful of boats without quantifying. ON THE THESIS. The outside-Alaska half is well supported by structure rather than by grievance. The company is in El Segundo, the plant is 16,000 square feet in Tacoma bought from FATHOM Seafood, the brand is Seremoni, and Khawaja says in his own words that Shinkei handles and markets the fish under its own brand. That is defensible. But the value-captured-outside claim is directly complicated by two verified facts the deck MUST carry. Khawaja says the machines go on the boats for free, and he says the company splits proceeds variably with the fishermen it works with, while trade coverage of the Alaska rollout says Shinkei buys the catch at a premium. The honest frame is that the fishermen appear to get more than the commodity price for these fish while the brand, the shelf-life asset, the data and the margin all live downstream and out of state. ON THE PRICE SPREAD. Do not attempt one. The single Cook Inlet number that survived, roughly 1.73 dollars a pound in 2025, is a Deckboss estimate and must be hedged and dated. Never substitute the Bristol Bay 1.60 base price for Cook Inlet. ON THE AI FRAMING. Every performance number in this deck, 3x shelf life, 60 hours, 70 percent, six seconds, comes from Shinkei. Attribute all of them. SOURCING. Thirty claims, all thirty carry a source_url, all thirty were fetched, seven are primary.
